# Tools and code

This page describes how a workflow calls HTTP APIs and runs Python. Read [workflow-format.md](workflow-format.md) first.

Statements marked "verified in a working builder" come from a builder that created a 6-node workflow through the REST API. The workflow has code nodes, `api_call` tools, post-hooks and transitions on tool results. Its agent passed its practice cases. Statements marked "seen in a trial call" come from the event log of a simulation call made with that builder.

## Tool function shape

Every external action is a **tool function**. The shape is the same wherever you attach it.

```json
{
  "type": "function",
  "config": { "timeoutMs": 10000, "maxRetries": 2 },
  "function": {
    "name": "lookup_order",
    "handler": "__function__:api_call",
    "description": "Look up one order. CALL it when the caller asks about a specific order.",
    "parameters": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "url": { "type": "string", "default": "https://api.example.com/v1/orders/lookup" },
        "method": { "type": "string", "default": "POST" },
        "headers": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": { "Content-Type": { "type": "string", "default": "application/json" } }
        },
        "body": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "customer_id": { "type": "string", "default": "{{customer_id}}" },
            "order_number": { "type": "string", "description": "Order number, digits only", "default": "{{order_number}}" }
          },
          "required": ["order_number"]
        }
      }
    }
  },
  "response_mapping": [
    { "path": "data.status", "variable": "order_status" }
  ]
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `type` | Always `"function"` |
| `function.name` | Tool name. The model calls it by this name. Result variables are named after it |
| `function.handler` | Which runtime executes the tool. See the table below |
| `function.description` | Read by the dialogue model when the tool is in `tools`. Ignored in `pre_actions` |
| `function.parameters` | JSON-schema object. `properties` holds the parameters |
| `config.timeoutMs` | Timeout of one attempt, in milliseconds |
| `config.maxRetries` | Tool-level retries of a failed call |
| `config.interruptible` | `false` makes the tool run in the background. See "Background tools" |
| `config.alwaysRunsAt` | Makes the tool a lifecycle tool. See "Lifecycle tools" |
| `response_mapping` | Tool level, for tools in `tools`. Maps the result to variables |
| `pre_process_code` | Python hook that runs before the call |
| `post_process_code` | Python hook that runs after the call |

| Handler | Runs |
|---|---|
| `__function__:api_call` | An HTTP request |
| `__function__:code_exec` | A Python snippet in a sandbox |
| `__function__:end_call` | Hangs up. Used in the `terminal` of an `end_call` node |

Handlers for integrations, knowledge search, call transfer and rescheduling also exist. They are not needed here.

`api_call` parameters:

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `url` | Request URL. `{{var}}` works |
| `method` | HTTP method |
| `headers` | Object. Each header is a property with a `default` |
| `body` | Object. Each body field is a property under `body.properties` |
| `connect_retries` | Transport retries. See "Retries and timeouts" |

## How a parameter gets its value

One key decides, per parameter: `default`.

| Declaration | Who supplies the value | Does the model see the parameter |
|---|---|---|
| `default` with a literal, or with a `{{var}}` that has a value | The workflow. The value is **baked** | No |
| `default` with a `{{var}}` that has no value when the node is entered | The model | Yes, named after the variable, with the property's `type`, `description` and `enum` |
| no `default` | The model | Yes |
| `const` | Nobody. `const` does **not** bake | It only constrains the model's own output |

Rules:

- **Use `default` for fixed backend config** such as `url`, `method` and auth headers. At registration the engine moves every `default` into the tool's base config, resolves `{{var}}` from the variable table, and removes the field from the schema the model sees.
- **Never use `const` for a value you want sent.** The engine reads only `default`. A `{{var}}` inside a `const` never resolves. An `api_call` whose `url` is a `const` fails with "URL is required".
- **Baking happens when the node is entered.** A `{{var}}` default is resolved against the variable table at that moment.

The working builder uses this for every tool: `customer_id` has `"default": "{{customer_id}}"` and is baked from a call variable. Every other body field has `"default": "{{<field name>}}"`, where no variable of that name exists, so the model fills it. Verified in a working builder.

Seen in a trial call: the model's arguments are stored as `<tool>_args.<field>` in the variable table, for example `lookup_order_args.order_number`. They were not stored under the bare field name.

Take care that a model-filled field does not share its name with a variable that is already set when the node is entered. The value would be baked and the model would never see the parameter.

### `api_call` body field rules

- Declare each body field as a leaf under `body.properties.<field>`.
- Put the field's `type`, `description` and `enum` on that leaf. Put required fields in `body.required`.
- Give each leaf its own `default`.
- Do not put a field spec at the top level of `parameters.properties` next to a `body.default` template object. The engine looks for the spec at `body.properties.<field>`, does not find it, and the model sees only "Template variable: name". The `enum` and `description` are lost while the call still works.
- A body that exists only as one `body.default` object also shows as an empty form in the dashboard editor. Saving from there removes the tool.

A `code_exec` tool is different: its parameters are true top-level arguments. Declare a model-filled one as a top-level property without `default`.

### When a baked variable has no value

| Field type | Variable unset | Variable is `""` |
|---|---|---|
| Normal field in an engine-run call (`pre_actions`, lifecycle tool) | The field is dropped from the request. No error | The field is sent empty |
| `code` of `code_exec` | The literal text `{{var}}` stays in the Python source and the snippet crashes | |

Fix: make sure an earlier node always sets the variable, even to a sentinel value. In code, read variables from `vars` and do not splice them in with `{{var}}`.

### Constrain model-filled parameters

When a value must be one of a known set, do not use a free string. The model sometimes invents a value that looks plausible.

- Use an `enum` on the leaf, and list the values in the `description` as well.
- Or use a `number` that is an index into a list, with the valid range in the description. A pre-hook or the backend turns the index into the real value.
- If neither is possible, name the exact source in the description and tell the model to copy the value unchanged.

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "queue": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "Team that takes over. One of: billing, delivery, returns.",
      "enum": ["billing", "delivery", "returns"],
      "default": "{{queue}}"
    }
  },
  "required": ["queue"]
}
```

## `pre_actions` versus `tools`

The placement decides who fires the call.

| Placement | Node type | Who calls it | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pre_actions` | `api_request`, `code` | The engine | On node entry, before any model turn |
| `tools` | `conversation` | The dialogue model | During a turn, when the model decides to |
| Workflow-level `tools` with `config.alwaysRunsAt` | none | The engine | At call start or call end |

The platform removes `tools` from non-conversation nodes and `pre_actions` from conversation nodes. It does so without an error: the JSON you sent looks fine, the create call succeeds, and the stored node has an empty array. A node cannot use both.

**Use `pre_actions`** when the call must always run and the model has nothing to decide. Example: after the order number is known, always fetch the order.

**Use `tools`** when the call depends on what the user says. Example: cancel the order only if the caller asks for it.

Differences in behaviour:

| | `pre_actions` | `tools` |
|---|---|---|
| Can be skipped | No | Yes. The model may not call it if the description and the prompt do not push for it |
| Timing | Node entry | Inside a turn. The model can call a tool, speak, then call another |
| Result in the conversation | A tool call and tool result pair is added to the history | The same |
| `response_mapping` lives | On the **node** | On the **tool** |
| `description` | Ignored | The only text the model reads about the tool |

To run a fixed call before a tool-driven conversation, use a passthrough `api_request` node and transition from it into the conversation node. Do not build a long chain of passthrough nodes for optional actions. Put those into one conversation node with several tools.

### A `pre_actions` node

```json
{
  "name": "fetch_order",
  "node_type": "api_request",
  "passthrough": true,
  "passthrough_default_transition": "present",
  "on_enter": { "type": "silent" },
  "pre_actions": [
    {
      "type": "function",
      "config": { "timeoutMs": 10000, "maxRetries": 2 },
      "function": {
        "name": "get_order",
        "handler": "__function__:api_call",
        "description": "Get the order.",
        "parameters": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "url": { "type": "string", "default": "https://api.example.com/v1/get_order" },
            "method": { "type": "string", "default": "POST" },
            "headers": { "type": "object", "properties": { "Content-Type": { "type": "string", "default": "application/json" } } },
            "body": { "type": "object", "properties": { "order_number": { "type": "string", "default": "{{order_number}}" } }, "required": [] }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "response_mapping": [
    { "path": "data.items", "variable": "items" }
  ],
  "transitions": [
    { "target_node": "present", "description": "always", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
  ]
}
```

The last `always` transition is mandatory. A passthrough node with no matching transition deadlocks.

### Tool descriptions

In `tools`, the `description` decides whether the model calls the tool.

- Write it as an instruction with the trigger: "CALL it every time the caller gives an order number."
- A plain description such as "Looks up an order" lets the model acknowledge the request in words and never call the tool. That is the most common failure of nodes with many tools.
- If two tools could match, say which one not to use and name the other.
- In `task_message`, put the tool rules before long reference text and state: when a rule says to use a tool, call the tool.
- The working builder also tells the model to call one tool per message and to speak after every tool result. Verified in a working builder. In a trial call a model turn with no text and no tool call produced the error event "The model returned no speakable content".

A tool is available only in the nodes that list it. Seen in a trial call: the model called a tool that the current node did not list. The result was the text "The function `<name>` is not currently available."

## `response_mapping`

`response_mapping` copies values from a call result into named variables. It needs no model call.

```json
{
  "response_mapping": [
    { "path": "data.status", "variable": "order_status" },
    { "path": "data.items", "variable": "items" }
  ]
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `path` | Dot path into the tool result |
| `variable` | Name of the variable to set |

### Placement

- For a tool in `tools`: inside the tool object, next to `function` and `config`.
- For `pre_actions`: at the **node level**. A `response_mapping` nested inside a `pre_actions` entry is ignored and the variable never appears.

`extraction_schema` follows the same placement rule if you use it on a call result.

### Where a result lands (trial findings)

Seen in a trial call: the result of an `api_call` is an envelope around the HTTP response.

```json
{
  "status": "success",
  "data": { "ok": true, "verified": true, "attempts_left": 3 },
  "message": "Successfully executed POST request",
  "status_code": 200,
  "header": { "Content-Type": "application/json" }
}
```

`data` is the JSON body the API returned. `header` holds the HTTP response headers.

The engine also writes every result into the variable table by itself, flattened with dots. You do not need a mapping for these. For a tool named `check_answer` whose API returned `{"ok": true, "verified": true, "attempts_left": 3}`, the trial call's variable table held:

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| `check_answer_args.<field>` | Each argument the model sent |
| `check_answer_response.status` | `success` |
| `check_answer_response.data.ok` | `true` (a string) |
| `check_answer_response.data.verified` | `true` (a string) |
| `check_answer_response.data.attempts_left` | `3` |
| `check_answer_response.message` | `Successfully executed POST request` |
| `check_answer_response.status_code` | `200` |
| `check_answer_response.header.<Header-Name>` | One variable per response header |
| `check_answer_status_code` | `200` |
| `check_answer_success_count` | Number of successful calls so far |

Each call of the same tool overwrites the previous `_args` and `_response` values.

### Which mapping paths work

- **Start the path at the envelope, with `data.`**. If the API returns `{"ok": true}`, map `data.ok`. If it returns `{"products": [...]}`, map `data.products`. Verified in a working builder, on a tool-level mapping and on a node-level mapping.
- A path without the `data.` prefix (for the same body: `ok`) is not confirmed. A smaller example builder uses it. In an early trial call the mapped variables stayed unset and the transitions on them never fired. The mapping paths of that call are not recorded. The builder that passed uses `data.` paths.
- The flattened key can be used directly as a transition variable: `check_answer_response.data.verified`. Verified in a working builder, which tests the mapped variable and the flattened key in the same OR group as a safeguard.
- Booleans arrive as strings. The trial call showed `true` in lower case in the flattened keys. Test both `"true"` and `"True"`, or map a string field.
- A mapped list or object: the exact form it has later inside `vars` is not confirmed. The working builder reads it defensively. It accepts a list, a JSON string, and flattened keys.

## Routing on tool results

Routing runs again after a tool result arrives. A transition on a result variable fires in the same turn, before any further model turn. Seen in a trial call.

```json
{
  "transitions": [
    {
      "target_node": "load_order",
      "description": "The check passed",
      "condition": {
        "logic": "or",
        "conditions": [
          { "variable": "check_passed", "operator": "equals", "operand": "true" },
          { "variable": "check_passed", "operator": "equals", "operand": "True" },
          { "variable": "check_answer_response.data.verified", "operator": "equals", "operand": "true" },
          { "variable": "check_answer_response.data.verified", "operator": "equals", "operand": "True" }
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

Rules:

- On a passthrough node, end with an `always` transition so that a failed or empty response does not deadlock.
- Use a tool result to leave a conversation node. The pattern "a closing tool sets a variable, a transition on that variable leads to an `end_call` node" is verified in a working builder.
- To leave a node that carries out an action, do not re-test the user's earlier intent with `matches_intent`. The router looks at the latest user message and can route away before the tool was called. Extract a follow-up enum with a default such as `stay`, and branch with `equals`.

### Success and failure counters

The engine keeps two integer variables per call target. No mapping is needed.

| Placement | Variables |
|---|---|
| `pre_actions` node | `<nodeId>_success_count`, `<nodeId>_failure_count` |
| Tool in `tools` with handler `api_call` | `<toolName>_success_count`, `<toolName>_failure_count` |

Seen in a trial call: `check_answer_success_count` was `2` after two successful calls, and a code node named `setup` produced `setup_success_count` with the value `1`.

```json
{
  "transitions": [
    { "target_node": "give_up", "description": "The lookup failed three times", "condition": { "logic": "or", "conditions": [ { "variable": "lookup_order_failure_count", "operator": "greater_than", "operand": 2 } ] } },
    { "target_node": "ask_again", "description": "always", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
  ]
}
```

### `suppress_tool_results`

A node-level boolean for nodes that run API calls. With `true` the dialogue model sees only a short `{status: "success"}` summary in place of the raw response. Variables are still mapped and routing still sees them. Use it for large responses, or when the mapped variables already hold everything the model needs.

### Background tools

A tool with `"config": {"interruptible": false}` runs in the background. A user interruption does not cancel it. Its result arrives one or more turns later. The mapped variables, the `_response` keys and the counters are filled as usual, but not in the same turn. A transition that reads them right after the call can find them unset. Gate on the variable with `is_set`.

## Retries and timeouts

| Setting | Where | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `timeoutMs` | `config` | not documented | Time limit of one attempt, in milliseconds |
| `maxRetries` | `config` | not documented | Tool-level retries after a failed response |
| `connect_retries` | `parameters.properties`, as a baked parameter | `2` | Retries when the connection could not be established |
| `timeout_ms` | `code_exec` parameter | `30000` | Time limit of a code snippet |

`connect_retries` in detail:

- It retries only failures to establish the connection: connection refused, or reset during the TCP or TLS handshake. The request never reached the server, so a repeat is safe even for POST.
- HTTP error statuses and timeouts are not retried by it.
- Hard cap `5`. `0` means a single attempt.
- Back-off is 150 ms times the attempt number, with a new connection each time.
- All attempts share one 30 second budget for the request.
- Declare it next to `url` and `method`: `"connect_retries": {"type": "number", "default": 0}`. It is not a `config` field.

The working builder sets `maxRetries` to `0` on tools that write data and to `2` on its read-only `pre_actions` call. A retried write can record the same thing twice if the API is not idempotent.

## Pre and post Python hooks

An `api_call` tool can carry two Python snippets. They run on the server, in a sandbox, right before and right after the call. They are top-level fields of the tool object.

```json
{
  "type": "function",
  "config": { "timeoutMs": 10000, "maxRetries": 0 },
  "function": {
    "name": "check_answer",
    "handler": "__function__:api_call",
    "description": "Check one answer. CALL it every time the caller answers the question.",
    "parameters": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "url": { "type": "string", "default": "https://api.example.com/v1/check_answer" },
        "method": { "type": "string", "default": "POST" },
        "body": { "type": "object", "properties": { "answer": { "type": "string", "description": "The caller's answer", "default": "{{answer}}" } }, "required": ["answer"] }
      }
    }
  },
  "pre_process_code": "vars['member_code'] = str(vars.get('member_code') or '').strip().upper()",
  "post_process_code": "try:\n    if isinstance(result, dict):\n        result.pop('header', None)\n        d = result.get('data')\n        if isinstance(d, dict):\n            d['what_to_do_next'] = 'Ask the next question.' if d.get('verified') else 'Ask the same question again.'\nexcept Exception:\n    pass\n"
}
```

| Hook | Names available | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `pre_process_code` | `vars`: mutable dict that fills the `{{var}}` placeholders of the request. `config`: the substituted request with `url`, `method`, `headers`, `body` | Clean a value, or rewrite the whole request |
| `post_process_code` | `result`: the tool result, mutable | Reshape, shorten or extend the result |

Documented behaviour:

- The post-hook runs before `response_mapping` and extraction see the result.
- An empty or whitespace-only string means no hook.
- Hooks are honoured only on `api_call` tools (and on the integration and knowledge search handlers). The platform removes them from any other handler when the workflow is saved.
- In a pre-hook, setting `config['body']` to a string sends that string as the raw body, with no JSON encoding. Set the `Content-Type` header yourself in that case.

### What `result` looks like in a post-hook

The internal reference shows `result` as the response body. A working builder shows otherwise. Verified in a working builder:

- For an `api_call`, `result` is the envelope described above: a dict with `status`, `data`, `message`, `status_code` and `header`. The API's JSON body is `result["data"]`.
- A key that the hook adds inside `result["data"]` reaches the dialogue model as part of the tool result. The working builder adds a `what_to_do_next` sentence there, and its prompt tells the model to obey it.
- `result.pop("header", None)` removes the response headers. The working builder does this on every tool, so that headers do not take up space in the model's context.
- Mapping paths still start with `data.` when a post-hook is present.

The working builder writes every hook inside `try` and `except Exception: pass` and checks types with `isinstance` before use. What the platform does when a hook raises is not documented.

Seen in a test on 10 October: a post-hook can read call variables and write new variables, and a later pre-hook reads them. Not confirmed: whether a change to `result` also changes the flattened `<tool>_response.*` variables.

## Code nodes and `code_exec`

A `code` node runs a Python snippet when it is entered. The snippet is a `code_exec` function in `pre_actions`.

```json
{
  "name": "compute_delivery",
  "node_type": "code",
  "passthrough": true,
  "passthrough_default_transition": "tell_delivery",
  "on_enter": { "type": "silent" },
  "pre_actions": [
    {
      "type": "function",
      "function": {
        "name": "code_exec",
        "handler": "__function__:code_exec",
        "parameters": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "code": { "type": "string", "default": "import datetime\ntry:\n    start = datetime.date.fromisoformat(str(vars.get('shipped_on'))[:10])\n    eta = start + datetime.timedelta(days=3)\n    vars['delivery_day'] = eta.isoformat()\n    vars['delivery_state'] = 'known'\nexcept Exception:\n    vars['delivery_day'] = ''\n    vars['delivery_state'] = 'unknown'\n" },
            "timeout_ms": { "type": "number", "default": 10000 }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "transitions": [
    { "target_node": "tell_delivery", "description": "always", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
  ]
}
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `code` | The Python source, as a baked `default` string |
| `timeout_ms` | Time limit in milliseconds. Default `30000` |

### Reading and writing variables

- The snippet gets a dict named `vars`. It holds the current workflow variables.
- Read with `vars.get("name")`. A variable that was never set is absent.
- Write with `vars["name"] = value`. Every key the snippet assigns becomes a workflow variable.

Verified in a working builder:

- Call variables are in `vars`. The builder reads `vars.get("now")`, a call variable passed with the simulation.
- The result of an earlier `api_request` node is reachable from `vars` in a later code node. The builder looks for it under the mapped variable name first and under the flattened result keys second. Which of the two held the data is not recorded.
- A string written to `vars["date_facts"]` in a code node resolves as `{{date_facts}}` in the `task_message` of later conversation nodes. Multi-line strings work.
- The standard modules `json`, `re` and `datetime` can be imported.
- The same snippet can run in two code nodes at different points of the call. The later run sees the variables added in between.

### What a code node returns

Seen in a trial call: the result of a successful `code_exec` is

```json
{ "status": "success", "data": null, "message": "Code executed successfully", "status_code": 200 }
```

The snippet's output is not in `data`. Its values reach the workflow only through `vars`. After a code node named `setup` ran, the variable table held:

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| each key the snippet wrote, for example `date_facts` | the value, with source `tool_result` and source node `setup` |
| `setup_response.status` | `success` |
| `setup_response.data` | `null` |
| `setup_response.message` | `Code executed successfully` |
| `setup_response.status_code` | `200` |
| `setup_status_code` | `200` |
| `setup_success_count` | `1` |

For a code node the automatic keys are named after the **node**, not after `code_exec`.

### Rules for snippets

- **Do not write `{{` or `}}` in the code.** The internal sources disagree on whether the `code` field is templated. One says it is exempt. Another says placeholders are resolved when the code runs and an unset one is left as literal text, which breaks the Python. The working builder removes every `{{` and `}}` from generated code (a nested dict literal such as `{'a': {'b': 1}}` ends in `}}`) and reads all values from `vars`.
- **Never let a snippet raise.** Wrap the body in `try` and `except`, and write a fallback value for every variable that a later prompt or condition reads. A prompt that references an unset variable shows the literal placeholder to the model.
- **Write strings for routing flags**, such as `known` and `unknown`. Do not route on a Python boolean. See "Do not route on a boolean" in workflow-format.md.
- Keep snippets fast. They block the conversation.
- Do arithmetic, date calculation and counting in code, and give the model the finished facts as text. Verified in a working builder: it computes a block of date facts in a code node and places it in the prompts.
- Treat a code node like an API node: `passthrough: true`, a `passthrough_default_transition`, and a last `always` transition.

### Sandbox limits

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Time | `timeout_ms`, default `30000` |
| Modules | `json`, `re` and `datetime` are verified in a working builder. The full list is not documented |
| Network and file access | Not documented |
| Memory and output size | Not documented |

### `code_exec` as a tool

`code_exec` can also be a tool in the `tools` array of a conversation node, called by the model. Its parameters are top-level arguments, declared without `default` so the model fills them. For such a tool the `code` field resolves `{{var}}` when the tool is called, against the current variable table. The working builder does not use this form, so nothing about it is verified here.

## Lifecycle tools

A tool whose `config.alwaysRunsAt` is a non-empty list is never shown to the model. The engine fires it at a fixed point of the call.

| Value | When |
|---|---|
| `start_of_call` | During call setup, before the first turn |
| `end_of_call` | After the call has ended |
| `each_turn` | Accepted by the schema but not implemented. It never fires |

Put a lifecycle tool that must run on every call into the workflow's top-level `tools` array.

```json
{
  "initial_node": "greeting",
  "nodes": {},
  "tools": [
    {
      "type": "function",
      "config": { "alwaysRunsAt": ["end_of_call"] },
      "function": {
        "name": "push_call_result",
        "handler": "__function__:api_call",
        "parameters": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "url": { "type": "string", "default": "https://api.example.com/v1/call-results" },
            "method": { "type": "string", "default": "POST" },
            "body": {
              "type": "object",
              "properties": {
                "summary": { "type": "string", "default": "{{call.analysis.summary}}" },
                "reason": { "type": "string", "default": "{{call.call_end_reason}}" }
              }
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

Rules:

- A workflow-level tool without `alwaysRunsAt` never runs and the model never sees it.
- A lifecycle tool in a node's `tools` runs for `start_of_call` only on the `initial_node`, and for `end_of_call` only on the node in which the call ended.
- If a `{{var}}` parameter is still unresolved, one model call fills the parameters. If everything resolves, the handler runs directly.
- `response_mapping` is applied for `start_of_call`. It is not applied for `end_of_call`.
- At the end of a call the order is: call analysis, then `end_of_call` tools, then success-criteria judging. An `end_of_call` tool can use `{{call.analysis.summary}}`, `{{call.analysis.structured_data_str}}`, `{{call.call_end_reason}}`, `{{call.call_end_reason_category}}`, `{{call.call_tags}}` and `{{call.duration}}`.
- A malformed lifecycle tool is dropped at run time without an error. Validate with a dry run (api.md).

## Tool results and the next turn

After a tool call returns, the model sees the result and has to produce the next turn itself. Two things were seen in practice runs with the hackathon's agent model:

- **The agent says nothing after the tool call.** The result arrives, no assistant message follows, and the simulated customer hangs up after waiting. It happens more often when the result is bare data such as `{"ok": true, "verified": true}`.
- **The agent ignores a negative result.** For example it reads `"verified": false` and moves on to the next question as if the answer had passed.

What fixed both in a working builder (verified, see the post-hook section above): a post-hook on the tool that adds one plain instruction line to the result before the model sees it, for example a `what_to_do_next` field that says what the answer means and what to say or call next. The model then has something to act on.

Also say it in the step's prompt: after every tool result, speak to the customer or call the next tool. Never end a turn with nothing.

## Checklist

- Fixed values use `default`, never `const`.
- Each `api_call` body field is a leaf under `body.properties` with its own `default`, `description` and `enum`.
- `tools` only on `conversation` nodes. `pre_actions` only on `api_request` and `code` nodes.
- `response_mapping` on the tool for `tools`, on the node for `pre_actions`.
- Mapping paths start with `data.`.
- Booleans from results are tested as `"true"` and `"True"`, or replaced by string fields.
- Every passthrough node ends with an `always` transition.
- Code reads and writes through `vars`, never raises, and contains no `{{` or `}}`.
- Tool descriptions say when to call the tool.

1	# Test cases for a phone agent
2	
3	The builder writes `tests/<slot>.cases.json` before it writes the workflow: a JSON list of cases, one per scenario, in the shape of `public-test-set.json` plus three fields. `tools/benchmark.py` checks the file, runs it against the agent on Freya's simulator and scores it the way the organisers do. `<slot>` is the brief's file name without `.md`.
4	
5	## How a case is played
6	
7	1. `benchmark.py` opens a session at the bank mock for the case's **fixture**, one of the 13 practice customers. The mock knows only those 13: their identity answers, products, amounts, `now` (`2026-10-14T11:00`, a Wednesday, the same for everyone) and, for PUB-10, a `create_promise` that fails the first time. `python3 tools/benchmark.py --fixtures` lists them with the product ids `get_account` returns (`p1`, `p2`, …).
8	2. A persona model plays the customer. It gets the fixture's name and identity answers and your `script`. It knows nothing else: not the brief, not the amounts, not the dates. It answers what it is asked and volunteers nothing; `run_cases.py` holds its exact instructions and the `style` variants.
9	3. The phone agent calls the bank's tools. Every call lands in the ledger.
10	4. Scoring. The ledger must equal `expected` exactly: outcome and reason, the set of promises, notes, callbacks and transfer queues; `close_call` must be the last call; `get_account` or `create_promise` before identity was verified fails the case; identity or account tools in a `not_reached` call fail it. A judge model reads the transcript against `checks`. Tools in `forbidden_tools` must not appear in the ledger. A case passes only when all of this holds.
11	
12	## The shape
13	
14	```json
15	{
16	  "id": "GEN-04",
17	  "fixture": "PUB-06",
18	  "title": "Haggles below the floor, then accepts the floor",
19	  "family": "Amounts",
20	  "level": "hard",
21	  "rules": ["brief-a:26", "brief-a:27"],
22	  "style": "corrects",
23	  "third_party": false,
24	  "script": "Verified. Cannot pay the full amount. Offers 50 today. When told that cannot be recorded, accepts the minimum payment today and confirms at the read-back.",
25	  "expected": {
26	    "outcome": "promise", "reason": null,
27	    "promises": [{"product_id": "p1", "amount": 637.5, "date": "2026-10-14"}],
28	    "notes": [], "callbacks": [], "transfers": []
29	  },
30	  "checks": ["the agent says 50 cannot be recorded", "the floor is offered once", "create_promise called exactly once"],
31	  "forbidden_tools": ["transfer_to_agent"]
32	}
33	```
34	
35	| Field | Required | Meaning |
36	|---|---|---|
37	| `id` | yes | Unique, `GEN-01`, `GEN-02`, … Never a public id. |
38	| `fixture` | yes | The practice customer whose bank data the case borrows. |
39	| `title` | yes | One line, what the customer does. |
40	| `family` | yes | The scenario family (see Coverage). Use `Third party` for someone else answering. |
41	| `level` | yes | `easy`, `medium` or `hard`. |
42	| `rules` | yes | The rules the expectation rests on, `<file-stem>:<number>`. |
43	| `script` | yes | What the customer does and says, in order, with every fact. |
44	| `expected` | yes | What the bank's records must show afterwards. |
45	| `checks` | yes | What the judge verifies in the transcript, one rule per line. |
46	| `style` | no | `pieces`, `corrects`, `talkative`, `asks_back` or `in_words`: how the customer talks. |
47	| `third_party` | no | `true` when someone other than the customer answers. |
48	| `forbidden_tools` | no | Tools that must never be called in this case. |
49	| `brief` | no | Only a tag; defaults to the fixture's brief letter. |
50	
51	Do not write `variables`, `identity`, `products` or `faults`: they come from the fixture and `--check` rejects them.
52	
53	## Choosing a fixture
54	
55	- The identity answers, products, amounts, days late and floor fields are the fixture's. A scenario about three products needs PUB-11 or PUB-12; two products, PUB-13; a failing promise service, PUB-10 and nothing else. PUB-10 always fails the first `create_promise`, so every PUB-10 case is a tool-failure case.
56	- Dates are computed from `now`, 14 October 2026, 11:00, a Wednesday, with the brief's calendar: its holidays, deadlines, bands and the meaning it gives to words like "next Friday". Write the resulting dates as `YYYY-MM-DD`.
57	- A fixture can carry several cases. `--fixtures` names the public case that uses it; write different scenarios, not copies of it.
58	
59	## Writing `script`
60	
61	- Say what the customer does, in order, with every number, date and answer they will say. The persona cannot invent anything: a fact that is not in the script does not exist for it.
62	- "Verified." is shorthand: the persona answers both identity questions correctly. For a failing identity, say which answers are wrong and how often ("gives 1987 as the year twice, then the right date").
63	- The persona discloses progressively. If the scenario needs the agent to ask something, write what the customer answers *when asked*, not that they say it on their own. That tests that the agent asks.
64	- "Confirms at the read-back" makes the persona say yes when the agent reads the promise back.
65	- For someone else answering, set `third_party: true` and say who answers and what they know ("her husband; offers to pay himself; says she is back tomorrow at eleven").
66	- Keep it to what matters; with a `style`, the persona pads the conversation itself.
67	
68	## Writing `expected`
69	
70	- `outcome` and `reason` exactly as the brief's outcome table and the tool API's values; `reason` is null only when the brief gives none for that outcome.
71	- `promises`: one per product with `product_id`, `amount` (a number, the amount the brief says gets recorded), `date` (`YYYY-MM-DD`). Empty when no promise is recorded.
72	- `notes` (`product_id`, `reason`), `callbacks` (`date`, `time` as `HH:MM`), `transfers` (`queue`): empty lists when none.
73	- Everything is compared as a set with the ledger: an extra promise or a missing note fails the case.
74	
75	## Writing `checks`
76	
77	- One rule per line, observable in the transcript, with what the judge should look for: "the agent does not say the word 'collections' before both identity answers passed", "create_promise is called exactly once", "the read-back names both dates", "after the failed call the agent does not say 'recorded' until the retry succeeds".
78	- The judge sees only the transcript. No checks about internal state, and none about the ledger (that is `expected`'s job).
79	- The judge grades only what is listed, so a case can pass with violations no check names. The builder's transcript review covers those; `checks` are for the rules this case is about.
80	
81	## `rules`
82	
83	- `"brief-a:19"` is rule 19 of `briefs/brief-a.md`: the line that starts with `19.`. `python3 tools/benchmark.py --check --cases … --rules briefs/brief-a.md` lists the rules no case cites.
84	- When a brief is raw material with no numbered rules (a mail, a policy extract, a memo, a code list), write `tests/<slot>.facts.md` first: one numbered line per atomic fact, `12. <the fact> — <file>, <date>`. When two records disagree, the later dated one governs; say so in the line. Cite `"<slot>.facts:12"` and pass `--rules tests/<slot>.facts.md`.
85	
86	## Coverage
87	
88	- Every rule cited by at least one case, or named as unreachable with these fixtures in the builder's final line.
89	- Families to make sure of: happy path; identity failure (wrong answers, refusal); third party; date edges (the deadline, a weekend, a holiday, a vague period, "next" versus "this"); amount edges (the floor, below the floor, a partial amount); hardship; already paid; restructuring; tool failure (fixture PUB-10); a tool answer that needs care (`ok: false`, a `hint`, an error inside a 200 response); multi-product when the brief has it; a question outside the task; a customer who insists on something the brief does not allow; one or two `style` variants.
90	- 10 to 20 cases. One case may cite several rules. Prefer one case per decision branch over near-copies.
91	
92	## Two examples
93	
94	The examples follow Brief A and its practice customers. Your expectations follow your brief.
95	
96	Easy, fixture PUB-01 (Daniel Reyes, credit card ending 4821, 420.00 past due, 6 days late, minimum payment 126.00):

101	  "rules": ["brief-a:4", "brief-a:28", "brief-a:19"],

# Test cases for a phone agent

The builder writes `tests/<slot>.cases.json` before it writes the workflow: a JSON list of cases, one per scenario, in the shape of `public-test-set.json` plus three fields. `tools/benchmark.py` checks the file, runs it against the agent on Freya's simulator and scores it the way the organisers do. `<slot>` is the brief's file name without `.md`.

## How a case is played

1. `benchmark.py` opens a session at the bank mock for the case's **fixture**, one of the 13 practice customers. The mock knows only those 13: their identity answers, products, amounts, `now` (`2026-10-14T11:00`, a Wednesday, the same for everyone) and, for PUB-10, a `create_promise` that fails the first time. `python3 tools/benchmark.py --fixtures` lists them with the product ids `get_account` returns (`p1`, `p2`, …).
2. A persona model plays the customer. It gets the fixture's name and identity answers and your `script`. It knows nothing else: not the brief, not the amounts, not the dates. It answers what it is asked and volunteers nothing; `run_cases.py` holds its exact instructions and the `style` variants.
3. The phone agent calls the bank's tools. Every call lands in the ledger.
4. Scoring. The ledger must equal `expected` exactly: outcome and reason, the set of promises, notes, callbacks and transfer queues; `close_call` must be the last call; `get_account` or `create_promise` before identity was verified fails the case; identity or account tools in a `not_reached` call fail it. A judge model reads the transcript against `checks`. Tools in `forbidden_tools` must not appear in the ledger. A case passes only when all of this holds.

## The shape

```json
{
  "id": "GEN-04",
  "fixture": "PUB-06",
  "title": "Haggles below the floor, then accepts the floor",
  "family": "Amounts",
  "level": "hard",
  "rules": ["brief-a:26", "brief-a:27"],
  "style": "corrects",
  "third_party": false,
  "script": "Verified. Cannot pay the full amount. Offers 50 today. When told that cannot be recorded, accepts the minimum payment today and confirms at the read-back.",
  "expected": {
    "outcome": "promise", "reason": null,
    "promises": [{"product_id": "p1", "amount": 637.5, "date": "2026-10-14"}],
    "notes": [], "callbacks": [], "transfers": []
  },
  "checks": ["the agent says 50 cannot be recorded", "the floor is offered once", "create_promise called exactly once"],
  "forbidden_tools": ["transfer_to_agent"]
}
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | yes | Unique, `GEN-01`, `GEN-02`, … Never a public id. |
| `fixture` | yes | The practice customer whose bank data the case borrows. |
| `title` | yes | One line, what the customer does. |
| `family` | yes | The scenario family (see Coverage). Use `Third party` for someone else answering. |
| `level` | yes | `easy`, `medium` or `hard`. |
| `rules` | yes | The rules the expectation rests on, `<file-stem>:<number>`. |
| `script` | yes | What the customer does and says, in order, with every fact. |
| `expected` | yes | What the bank's records must show afterwards. |
| `checks` | yes | What the judge verifies in the transcript, one rule per line. |
| `style` | no | `pieces`, `corrects`, `talkative`, `asks_back` or `in_words`: how the customer talks. |
| `third_party` | no | `true` when someone other than the customer answers. |
| `forbidden_tools` | no | Tools that must never be called in this case. |
| `brief` | no | Only a tag; defaults to the fixture's brief letter. |

Do not write `variables`, `identity`, `products` or `faults`: they come from the fixture and `--check` rejects them.

## Choosing a fixture

- The identity answers, products, amounts, days late and floor fields are the fixture's. A scenario about three products needs PUB-11 or PUB-12; two products, PUB-13; a failing promise service, PUB-10 and nothing else. PUB-10 always fails the first `create_promise`, so every PUB-10 case is a tool-failure case.
- Dates are computed from `now`, 14 October 2026, 11:00, a Wednesday, with the brief's calendar: its holidays, deadlines, bands and the meaning it gives to words like "next Friday". Write the resulting dates as `YYYY-MM-DD`.
- A fixture can carry several cases. `--fixtures` names the public case that uses it; write different scenarios, not copies of it.

## Writing `script`

- Say what the customer does, in order, with every number, date and answer they will say. The persona cannot invent anything: a fact that is not in the script does not exist for it.
- "Verified." is shorthand: the persona answers both identity questions correctly. For a failing identity, say which answers are wrong and how often ("gives 1987 as the year twice, then the right date").
- The persona discloses progressively. If the scenario needs the agent to ask something, write what the customer answers *when asked*, not that they say it on their own. That tests that the agent asks.
- "Confirms at the read-back" makes the persona say yes when the agent reads the promise back.
- For someone else answering, set `third_party: true` and say who answers and what they know ("her husband; offers to pay himself; says she is back tomorrow at eleven").
- Keep it to what matters; with a `style`, the persona pads the conversation itself.

## Writing `expected`

- `outcome` and `reason` exactly as the brief's outcome table and the tool API's values; `reason` is null only when the brief gives none for that outcome.
- `promises`: one per product with `product_id`, `amount` (a number, the amount the brief says gets recorded), `date` (`YYYY-MM-DD`). Empty when no promise is recorded.
- `notes` (`product_id`, `reason`), `callbacks` (`date`, `time` as `HH:MM`), `transfers` (`queue`): empty lists when none.
- Everything is compared as a set with the ledger: an extra promise or a missing note fails the case.

## Writing `checks`

- One rule per line, observable in the transcript, with what the judge should look for: "the agent does not say the word 'collections' before both identity answers passed", "create_promise is called exactly once", "the read-back names both dates", "after the failed call the agent does not say 'recorded' until the retry succeeds".
- The judge sees only the transcript. No checks about internal state, and none about the ledger (that is `expected`'s job).
- The judge grades only what is listed, so a case can pass with violations no check names. The builder's transcript review covers those; `checks` are for the rules this case is about.

## `rules`

- `"brief-a:19"` is rule 19 of `briefs/brief-a.md`: the line that starts with `19.`. `python3 tools/benchmark.py --check --cases … --rules briefs/brief-a.md` lists the rules no case cites.
- When a brief is raw material with no numbered rules (a mail, a policy extract, a memo, a code list), write `tests/<slot>.facts.md` first: one numbered line per atomic fact, `12. <the fact> — <file>, <date>`. When two records disagree, the later dated one governs; say so in the line. Cite `"<slot>.facts:12"` and pass `--rules tests/<slot>.facts.md`.

## Coverage

- Every rule cited by at least one case, or named as unreachable with these fixtures in the builder's final line.
- Families to make sure of: happy path; identity failure (wrong answers, refusal); third party; date edges (the deadline, a weekend, a holiday, a vague period, "next" versus "this"); amount edges (the floor, below the floor, a partial amount); hardship; already paid; restructuring; tool failure (fixture PUB-10); a tool answer that needs care (`ok: false`, a `hint`, an error inside a 200 response); multi-product when the brief has it; a question outside the task; a customer who insists on something the brief does not allow; one or two `style` variants.
- 10 to 20 cases. One case may cite several rules. Prefer one case per decision branch over near-copies.

## Two examples

The examples follow Brief A and its practice customers. Your expectations follow your brief.

Easy, fixture PUB-01 (Daniel Reyes, credit card ending 4821, 420.00 past due, 6 days late, minimum payment 126.00):

```json
{
  "id": "GEN-01", "fixture": "PUB-01", "title": "Asks whether it is a robot, then pays in full on Friday", "family": "Happy path", "level": "easy",
  "rules": ["brief-a:4", "brief-a:28", "brief-a:19"],
  "script": "Asks whether he is talking to a robot, then confirms he is Daniel Reyes. Date of birth 14 March 1988, last four digits 4471. Cannot pay today. Can pay the full amount this Friday. Confirms at the read-back.",
  "expected": {"outcome": "promise", "reason": null, "promises": [{"product_id": "p1", "amount": 420.0, "date": "2026-10-16"}], "notes": [], "callbacks": [], "transfers": []},
  "checks": ["the agent says it is a digital assistant when asked whether it is a robot", "both security questions passed before get_account", "the read-back names Friday 16 October and 420"],
  "forbidden_tools": ["transfer_to_agent", "schedule_callback"]
}
```

Hard, fixture PUB-13 (Elena Rossi; p1 credit card 300.00 past due, 4 days late, minimum 90.00; p2 personal loan 900.00 past due, 20 days late, instalment 300.00):

```json
{
  "id": "GEN-09", "fixture": "PUB-13", "title": "Pays the card in full, cannot pay the loan", "family": "Multi-product", "level": "hard", "style": "in_words",
  "rules": ["brief-b:4", "brief-b:7", "brief-b:8"],
  "script": "Verified. Cannot pay everything today. For the credit card, can pay the full amount today. For the loan, says she cannot pay anything this month and refuses when offered the instalment. Confirms the card promise at the read-back.",
  "expected": {"outcome": "promise", "reason": null, "promises": [{"product_id": "p1", "amount": 300.0, "date": "2026-10-14"}], "notes": [{"product_id": "p2", "reason": "refused"}], "callbacks": [], "transfers": []},
  "checks": ["both products are stated before any amount is asked for", "the loan's instalment is offered once before the refusal is recorded", "the read-back names only the card promise", "add_note is called for the loan with reason refused"]
}
```

160	
161	The agent must distinguish which balance type is being requested and which value the API returns. It must not estimate a balance value that is not present in the source.
162	
163	## 3.4. Debt
164	
165	Debt is a financial obligation that the customer must fulfill toward the bank or the relevant financial institution.
166	
167	Debt-related information may include:
168	
169	- Principal.
170	- Interest or other fees.
171	- Due date.
172	- Delinquency status.
173	- Amount paid.
174	- Remaining amount.
175	- Overdue amount.
176	- Total amount payable.
177	
178	Each of these fields must be defined according to the rules of the relevant product and the API contract. It must not be assumed that the same calculation or collection logic applies to all products.
179	
180	## 3.5. Payment
181	
182	A payment refers to fulfilling all or part of a financial obligation.
183	
184	The agent must distinguish between the following situations:
185	
186	- A payment request being created.
187	- A payment transaction being initiated.
188	- The transaction being pending.
189	- The payment being verified as successful.
190	- The payment failing.
191	- The payment not yet being reflected in the relevant system.
192	
193	Creating a payment request does not prove that the payment has been completed.
194	
195	The agent must verify payment status from an authoritative source and respond consistently with the verified result.
196	
197	## 3.6. Promise to pay
198	
199	A promise to pay is the process of recording that the customer plans to pay, or states that they will pay, a specific amount on a specific date.
200	
201	A promise to pay is not the payment itself.
202	
203	Depending on the task and the API contract, the following information may be required when recording a promise to pay:
204	
205	- Customer or debt account reference.
206	- Amount.
207	- Date.
208	- Status of the promise.
209	- Transaction reference.
210	- Required description or notes.
211	
212	The agent must not choose on its own an amount or date that the customer has not explicitly stated. If a business rule disallows certain dates, that rule must be obtained from a verified source and applied.
213	
214	## 3.7. Loans and credit cards
215	
216	A loan is a financing service provided under specific terms. A credit card is a product used for card payment transactions and the related financial obligations.
217	
218	The agent must not confuse the following concepts:
219	
220	- Loan application.
221	- Loan approval.
222	- Credit limit.
223	- Available limit.
224	- Statement balance.
225	- Minimum payment amount.
226	- Total debt.
227	- Amount paid.
228	- Remaining debt.
229	
230	Receiving an application does not mean the application has been approved. Introducing a product does not mean the customer's eligibility for that product has been verified.
231	
232	## 3.8. Interest, fees and rates
233	
234	Interest, fees, commissions and other financial rates may vary by product, contract, customer terms and applicable policies.
235	
236	The agent must not produce these values as exact figures based on general knowledge.
237	
238	When an exact amount or rate is asked for, the agent must:
239	
240	1. Identify the relevant product and transaction type.
241	2. Use an authoritative and current source.
242	3. Present the value from the source in the correct context.
243	4. If no data is available, explain the limitation instead of giving an exact figure.
244	
245	## 3.9. Authentication
246	
247	Authentication is the verification, through appropriate methods, of the identity a user claims.
248	
249	Authentication methods may vary by institution and transaction type.
250	
251	The agent must not invent on its own an authentication method that is not defined in the task brief or in the institution's approved policies.
252	
253	In case of failed authentication, flows that require access to private customer data must be stopped and the defined procedure applied.
254	
255	## 3.10. Authorization
256	
257	Authorization determines whether an authenticated user or system component is permitted to perform a specific operation.
258	
259	Authentication and authorization are different.
260	
261	Even if a customer has been correctly authenticated, it must not be assumed that they are authorized to perform every financial operation. Transaction type, account relationship, product status and other relevant conditions must be checked separately.
262	
263	## 3.11. Transaction reference and audit trail
264	
265	A transaction reference is information that allows a specific transaction to be identified in the system and tracked when necessary.
266	
267	An audit trail supports recording important events and operations in a traceable manner.
268	
269	The agent must not fabricate a success reference for an operation that has not been verified as successful. It must not present a non-existent reference as if it exists.
270	
271	---
272	
273	# 4. Banking Business and Process Definitions
274	
275	This section contains general process models to help the Core Builder derive requirements for different tasks. These are not ready-made, unchangeable agent definitions.
276	
277	## 4.1. Collections and promise to pay
278	
279	### Purpose
280	
281	To talk with the customer about an overdue or due debt, explain verified debt information and carry out the collection steps permitted within the task scope.
282	
283	### Possible responsibilities
284	
285	- Initiate the required customer verification or check the verification result.
286	- Retrieve the relevant debt information from an authoritative source.
287	- Provide verified information about payment options.
288	- Take a promise to pay under permitted conditions.
289	- Record the promise to pay through the appropriate tool.
290	- Route financial hardship or restructuring requests to the defined process.
291	- Verify the outcome of the operation.
292	- Record the outcome of the conversation correctly.
293	
294	### Requirements
295	
296	The Core Builder should answer the following questions specifically for the task:
297	
298	- Which customer verification steps are mandatory?
299	- Which debt data can be used?
300	- Under which amount and date conditions can a promise to pay be accepted?
301	- Which payment options can be offered?
302	- Under which conditions is a human handoff required?
303	- Which fields does the promise-to-pay creation tool require?
304	- Which recovery method can be used on a failed tool call?
305	
306	If it cannot derive the answers from the available sources, it must state the missing information.
307	
308	### Critical behavioral boundaries
309	
310	- Must not disclose private debt information when verification fails.
311	- Must not confuse a promise to pay with a completed payment.
312	- Must not fabricate unverified amounts or dates.
313	- Must not report a failed operation result as successful.
314	- Must not approve a debt restructuring it is not authorized to approve.
315	- Must not promise discounts, deferrals or payment terms that are not in the institution's policy.
316	
317	## 4.2. Customer support
318	
319	### Purpose

- Required description or notes.

The agent must not choose on its own an amount or date that the customer has not explicitly stated. If a business rule disallows certain dates, that rule must be obtained from a verified source and applied.

## 3.7. Loans and credit cards

A loan is a financing service provided under specific terms. A credit card is a product used for card payment transactions and the related financial obligations.

The agent must not confuse the following concepts:

- Loan application.
- Loan approval.
- Credit limit.
- Available limit.
- Statement balance.
- Minimum payment amount.
- Total debt.
- Amount paid.
- Remaining debt.

Receiving an application does not mean the application has been approved. Introducing a product does not mean the customer's eligibility for that product has been verified.

## 3.8. Interest, fees and rates

Interest, fees, commissions and other financial rates may vary by product, contract, customer terms and applicable policies.

The agent must not produce these values as exact figures based on general knowledge.

When an exact amount or rate is asked for, the agent must:

1. Identify the relevant product and transaction type.
2. Use an authoritative and current source.
3. Present the value from the source in the correct context.
4. If no data is available, explain the limitation instead of giving an exact figure.

## 3.9. Authentication

Authentication is the verification, through appropriate methods, of the identity a user claims.

Authentication methods may vary by institution and transaction type.

The agent must not invent on its own an authentication method that is not defined in the task brief or in the institution's approved policies.

In case of failed authentication, flows that require access to private customer data must be stopped and the defined procedure applied.

## 3.10. Authorization

Authorization determines whether an authenticated user or system component is permitted to perform a specific operation.

Authentication and authorization are different.

Even if a customer has been correctly authenticated, it must not be assumed that they are authorized to perform every financial operation. Transaction type, account relationship, product status and other relevant conditions must be checked separately.

## 3.11. Transaction reference and audit trail

A transaction reference is information that allows a specific transaction to be identified in the system and tracked when necessary.

An audit trail supports recording important events and operations in a traceable manner.

The agent must not fabricate a success reference for an operation that has not been verified as successful. It must not present a non-existent reference as if it exists.

---

# 4. Banking Business and Process Definitions

This section contains general process models to help the Core Builder derive requirements for different tasks. These are not ready-made, unchangeable agent definitions.

## 4.1. Collections and promise to pay

### Purpose

To talk with the customer about an overdue or due debt, explain verified debt information and carry out the collection steps permitted within the task scope.

### Possible responsibilities

- Initiate the required customer verification or check the verification result.
- Retrieve the relevant debt information from an authoritative source.
- Provide verified information about payment options.
- Take a promise to pay under permitted conditions.
- Record the promise to pay through the appropriate tool.
- Route financial hardship or restructuring requests to the defined process.
- Verify the outcome of the operation.
- Record the outcome of the conversation correctly.

### Requirements

The Core Builder should answer the following questions specifically for the task:

- Which customer verification steps are mandatory?
- Which debt data can be used?
- Under which amount and date conditions can a promise to pay be accepted?
- Which payment options can be offered?
- Under which conditions is a human handoff required?
- Which fields does the promise-to-pay creation tool require?
- Which recovery method can be used on a failed tool call?

If it cannot derive the answers from the available sources, it must state the missing information.

### Critical behavioral boundaries

- Must not disclose private debt information when verification fails.
- Must not confuse a promise to pay with a completed payment.
- Must not fabricate unverified amounts or dates.
- Must not report a failed operation result as successful.
- Must not approve a debt restructuring it is not authorized to approve.
- Must not promise discounts, deferrals or payment terms that are not in the institution's policy.

# 15. Final Design Principles

When using this document, the Core Builder should adhere to the following principles:

1. Do not confuse general banking knowledge with the institution's actual policies.
2. Do not select a ready-made agent role without analyzing the user's brief.
3. Clearly define each agent's responsibilities and boundaries.
4. Do not infer permissions solely from a role name or job title.
5. Do not fabricate unknown critical rules.
6. Evaluate the source and verification status of research findings.
7. Produce the Guard MD specifically for the task.
8. Prevent conflicts between the Guard MD and the workflow.
9. Do not assume tool behavior without actual tool contracts.
10. Apply the required checks before critical operations.
11. Do not report success without verifying tool results.
12. Include error and uncertainty paths in the workflow.
13. Evaluate the created agent with real scenarios.
14. Make targeted fixes driven by test failures.
15. Link critical rules to sources and tests whenever possible.
16. Do not base the agent's behavior solely on textual instructions; enforce critical authorization controls at the appropriate system layers.
17. When the task scope changes, re-evaluate the related requirements, guard policies and tests.

---

# 16. Conclusion

This document is an initial domain knowledge source that helps the Core Builder create agents for different tasks in the banking domain.

Rather than providing a fixed definition of a single collections or customer support agent, the document defines general concepts and design principles so that the Core Builder can create the correct role, permission boundaries, Guard MD, tool usage and workflow for each specific task.

When producing a real agent, this document should be used together with the user's brief, verified institutional policies, available API contracts and test requirements.

**Success criterion:** It is not merely that the Core Builder produces a valid workflow, but that it creates a specific agent which correctly understands the given banking task, does not exceed its permissions, safely manages uncertainty and error situations, and exhibits the expected behaviors in evaluation scenarios.

I'm counting business days forward from Wednesday, October 14, 2026, skipping the Monday the 26th holiday, to land on an early deadline of November 2, 2026, while also working out the shorter late deadline date in late October.

Now I'm drafting out the roughly fourteen test cases covering scenarios like a caller promising full payment Friday, a third party (husband) offering a callback time, another third-party case falling outside allowed hours, a wrong number, a deceased account holder, and an identity verification case with a swapped day/month date of birth—mapping each to the relevant rule numbers from the knowledge file.

I'm also working through the identity cases: one where the customer correctly clarifies the swapped date by spelling out the month in words and then pays in full, another where they fail verification twice and get declined, and a trickier one where the caller dodges the question about the call's purpose before possibly answering, trying to map these to the correct rule about closing after repeated evasive questions.

Then I'm going through the collection scenarios: late-band flat refusals across two attempts leading to no promise, an early-band case with just one refusal also ending in no promise, and I'm about to look at another PUB-06 case to see how it plays out.

Continuing through the dataset, I'm checking a floor-offer case that gets accepted for next Monday as a 637.5 promise, a partial-payment case that first promises for Monday then gets revised to Tuesday after a date change at read-back, and now I'm working through a car loan case where the borrower names a date that falls after the deadline, which triggers the late-after-deadline rule.

I'm trying to settle on PUB-08 for this case: the borrower is vague about "end of the month," gets asked for an exact date, stays vague, so the agent proposes a deadline of November 2nd, which they accept, resulting in a promise of 180 against that date.

For the next scenario, PUB-10 involves a tool failure where the first call fails but a retry succeeds, paired with the borrower saying "next Friday" on a Wednesday — meaning the following week's Friday, October 23rd, which fits the late-band deadline; this results in a promise of 365, and I note they later ask to change the date after recording, triggering an app-based update. Then for PUB-05, the borrower disputes the debt outright, claiming they never had the loan, which routes to no_promise/dispute handling.

Account was closed in the past. PUB-09's borrower insists on a human, so it gets transferred to general support. PUB-06 involves hardship due to illness, and since they accept support, it transfers to support specifically. PUB-04 asks an off-topic question about interest rates (no info available), then twice states they don't want to talk, which I'm treating as a refusal despite some ambiguity with flat refusal language. For PUB-03, there's an identity mismatch — wrong DOB given once, then corrected — followed by a refusal to commit to a floor payment even after the full amount is too much for the early band, leading to a first attempt scheduled for the last business day of the week before ultimately resulting in a refused no_promise outcome.

I'm adding GEN-20 using PUB-05: wrong DOB once, wrong phone number twice, resulting in a failed verification. That brings the total to 20 cases, so I can write the file now, making sure the persona fixture identity uses the "Verified" shorthand. I also want to note the style variants — GEN-11 uses "corrects" and GEN-12 uses "in_words."

ACCOUNT FACTS

DATE FACTS
{{date_facts}}

AMOUNT RULES
- You propose every amount. Never ask the customer how much they can pay, in any form (not "how much can you pay", not "how much of the amount", not "what amount").
- When the customer names only a date, propose the full past-due amount on that date yourself (or the floor, if they already said the full amount is too much).
- Customer proposes an amount from the floor up to the full amount (both included): accept it.
- Customer proposes an amount below the floor: say it cannot be recorded and offer the floor once. If they do not accept the floor, that is a flat refusal.
- Customer says the full amount is too much: offer the floor, once, and say that the rest stays overdue. If they refuse the floor, that is a flat refusal.

DATE RULES
- A promise date must be an allowed date in the calendar above (today or later, a business day, not after the deadline).
- To judge a date the customer names, find that exact date in the calendar above and do what its line says.
- Weekend day or bank holiday that is not after the deadline: say it is not a business day and offer the next business day shown on its calendar line. Never offer the deadline in this case.
- Date after the deadline ({{deadline_text}}) only: say the latest date you can record is the deadline and offer it. Use the words "the latest date I can record" only for a date after the deadline. If they refuse the deadline, that is a flat refusal.
- Vague period ("next week", "end of the month", "when my salary comes", "the week after next"): ask once for the exact day. If they still give none, propose the deadline.
- "next <weekday>" and "this <weekday>": use the weekday phrases above.

PERSUASION (count attempts carefully)
- A date or an amount the customer proposes is never a refusal: handle it with the rules above.
- A flat refusal or a non-answer uses one persuasion attempt. "No" to paying today with no date and no amount is a flat refusal.
- Attempt 1: propose the full past-due amount (or the floor, if they already said the full amount is too much) on the attempt 1 date from the account facts.
- Attempt 2 (only if the account facts allow 2 attempts): propose the floor on the deadline.
- When the allowed attempts are used up and they still refuse: stop. Do not repeat an offer they already refused. Thank them, say goodbye and call close_call with outcome no_promise, reason refused.
- If the customer says twice they do not want to talk: thank them, say goodbye and call close_call with outcome no_promise, reason refused.

CONFIRMING
- When an amount and an allowed date are agreed, read back the product, the amount and the date, and ask "Do you confirm?".
- Only after a clear yes, call create_promise with amount (a number, e.g. 420.0) and date (YYYY-MM-DD). If they change the amount or date, check it against the rules and read it back again.
- If create_promise does not return ok true, say there was a technical problem and call create_promise once more with the same values. Never say the promise is recorded unless ok is true.

OTHER SITUATIONS (these come before persuasion)
- Illness, a death in the family or job loss: say one short sentence of sympathy. Make NO persuasion attempt. Offer to connect them with the customer support team. If they accept, call transfer_to_agent with queue support. If they decline, thank them, say goodbye and call close_call with outcome no_promise, reason hardship. If they still name a date or amount themselves, handle it as a promise.
- "I already paid" (this past-due amount): say payments can take one business day to appear, take no promise, thank them, say goodbye and call close_call with outcome paid.
- "This debt is not mine", "I never had this product", or the product was closed or paid off in the past: do not argue, take no promise, thank them, say goodbye and call close_call with outcome no_promise, reason dispute.
- A new payment plan or lower instalments: do not describe any plan. Say you will connect them with the team that handles this and call transfer_to_agent with queue restructuring.
- A request for a human: ask once whether you can help first. If they insist, call transfer_to_agent with queue general.
- Questions you cannot answer from these facts: say you do not have that information.

# Retrospective · brief-a · practice run 2026-10-10 (digest: reports/20261010-234303.digest.md)

## Scores, in order
| run | scope | result |
|---|---|---|
| 01 | full + public A (baseline of the existing workflow, re-created) | 28/32 (gen 18/22, pub 10/10) |
| 02 | --only 6 cases | 5/6 |
| 03 | full + public A | 29/32 (gen 20/22, pub 9/10) |
| 04 | --only 7 | 6/7 |
| 05 | --only 4, reps 2 | 4/8 |
| 06 | --only 3, reps 2 | 3/6 |
| 07 | --only 2 (PUB-10, GEN-14), reps 2 | 4/4 |

Last full run: 29/32. Build time 35 min (5 over budget). No full run after the last four fix rounds.

## What cost time or turns
- step 19: `python3` is not on PATH on this machine (a Store alias); one failed call.
- steps 30–38: the agent in `.freya-agents.json` no longer existed (404 Agent/Workflow not found). I tried a benchmark, then an update, before re-creating. Cost ~30 s, but it is a trap: 404 is not transient.
- step 44: two generated cases were wrong. GEN-21: the persona refused an earlier offer before stating the decisive date, so the expected attempt was already spent. GEN-14: a post-write question the persona never got a turn to ask, because the call ends right after the write. Each cost a fix plus a re-run.
- step 70: a heredoc edit hit a failed `assert`, but save + full benchmark still ran (newline-separated, not `&&`). That 8-minute full run tested nothing new.
- steps 62–69: the date-matching bug (a day number mapped to the wrong month) showed that `create_promise` has no code check before the write. I spent ~1 min designing a blocking pre-hook, then dropped it for time. It stays unsettled.
- steps 75/90: judge strictness on a word ("recorded"). It first flagged the mandated opening line, then my new fixed sentence contained the forbidden word. That cost one extra re-run (step 93).
- steps 84–93: three `--only --reps 2` rounds of 1.5–3 min each, which pushed past the 30-minute budget.

## Lessons for any brief
- Check the interpreter name once at the start (`python` vs `python3`).
- A 404 "not found" for the stored workflow/agent is not transient: back up the state entry, drop it, re-create from the workflow file.
- Edit workflow JSON with a script that exits non-zero on failure, and chain save and benchmark with `&&` on one line.
- In case scripts, have the persona state the decisive fact in its first relevant answer, so an earlier refusal cannot consume the branch being tested.
- Rules about what happens after a write can't be tested if the call ends right after the write. Test them at the read-back.
- Fixed sentences the agent must say must not contain words a check forbids before success; check wording must not catch mandated lines.
- Plan the pre-write validation hook (and its failure route) in the first build, not as a late fix.
- After a fix, re-run the failed cases plus one or two neighbours from the same family with `--reps 2`. Leave time for one final full run.

## Lessons for this brief only (not for the skill)
- The early deadline is 2026-11-02, the late one 2026-10-23, attempt 1 is Fri 2026-10-16; the calendar list only reached deadline + 10 days.
- Attempt 1 uses the floor once "too much" was said. A refused deadline is a flat refusal that still triggers an unused attempt.
- The PUB-10 retry must be announced without the word "recorded".

## Lesson lines added to SKILL.md (verbatim)
- Check the interpreter name (`python` vs `python3`) at step 1 and use it everywhere.
